slides: Absolute value. It shows up on the exam in expressions, in equations and in inequalities, and one idea runs the whole topic. Let's learn it.

slides.say: The absolute value of a number is its distance from zero. Five is five steps away from zero, so the absolute value of five is five. Negative seven is a negative number, but its distance from zero is seven steps. So the absolute value of negative seven is seven.
at: Negative seven is a negative number
So the absolute value of negative

slides: A distance is never negative. The way from my home to my friend's home isn't minus three kilometers. It's three kilometers. That's why an absolute value is always zero or positive.

slides.say: We write it with two straight bars, one on each side of the number. This is the absolute value of x.
So what do the bars do to a number? A positive number stays exactly the same. The absolute value of nine is nine, and the absolute value of fifteen is fifteen.
at: The absolute value of nine is nine

slides.say: A negative number becomes the same number, but positive. The absolute value of negative four is four, and the absolute value of negative three fifths is three fifths. With a plain number, the minus simply drops off.
at: The absolute value of negative four

slides.say: And zero? Zero isn't far from zero at all. It's right there. So the absolute value of zero is zero.
at: So the absolute value of zero

slides.say: But careful with letters, because a letter hides its sign. If x is negative three, then minus x is plus three. So the absolute value of x is three, which is minus x, not x. If x is five, the absolute value of x is five, which is x itself. So with a letter, the minus doesn't just drop off. First ask: is the letter positive or negative?

slides: When there's a whole expression inside the bars, the bars belong to the whole expression, not to each number inside it. So we calculate the inside first, and only then take the bars.

slides.say: For example, the absolute value of three plus, in brackets, negative ten. Inside first: three plus negative ten is three minus ten, which is negative seven. Its absolute value is seven.
at: Inside first: three plus negative ten

slides.say: What we must not do is turn the negative ten into ten first, and then add. That gives three plus ten, which is thirteen, a different number.
One more. The absolute value of five minus eleven. Inside first: five minus eleven is negative six, so the absolute value is six. Inside first, then the bars.
Now three rules. Rule one is really the definition: an absolute value is never negative. It can be zero, and it can be positive. So whenever you see bars, think zero or positive.
at: an absolute value is never negative

slides.say: Rule two: for a product, we can put the bars on the whole product, or on each factor, and we get the same result. The absolute value of the whole product, negative four times five, is the absolute value of negative twenty, which is twenty. And the absolute value of negative four, times the absolute value of five, is four times five, also twenty.
at: The absolute value of the whole product

slides.say: The same works for a fraction: bars on the top, and bars on the bottom. Negative twelve over three is negative four, and its absolute value is four. Twelve over three is also four.

Rule three is about a sum. The absolute value of the whole sum, a plus b, is smaller than or equal to the absolute value of a, plus the absolute value of b. It's fine if you don't remember this rule. If a question uses it, you can solve it by plugging in numbers or by understanding. But let's see why it's true.
at: Rule three is about a sum

slides.say: When a and b have the same sign, the two sides are equal. Negative three plus negative four is negative seven, and its absolute value is seven. Separately, three plus four is also seven.
When they have different signs, the left side is smaller. Negative three plus four is one. Separately, three plus four is seven. One is smaller than seven.
at: Negative three plus four is one

slides: Why? Taking each one separately makes both of them positive, so their sum is as big as it can be. When one of them is negative inside the bars, it eats part of the other one. So same signs, equal. Different signs, smaller.

slides.say: A very useful trick is to compare a number with its own absolute value. It tells you the sign. If the absolute value is bigger than the number, the number is negative. For example, the absolute value of negative four is four, and four is bigger than negative four.
at: If the absolute value is bigger than the number

slides.say: If the absolute value equals the number, the number is positive or zero. The absolute value of nine is nine, and the absolute value of zero is zero. Don't forget the zero.
at: If the absolute value equals the number

slides.say: If the absolute value equals minus the number, the number is negative or zero. For example, the absolute value of negative six is six, and minus negative six is six too.

And if the number is bigger than its absolute value? That never happens. A negative number is smaller than its absolute value, and a positive number is equal to it. So a given like that contradicts itself. These clues come up on the exam again and again, and they tell you at once whether a number is positive or negative.
Now equations. The absolute value of x equals six. Which numbers are six steps from zero? Six, and negative six. One on each side of zero.

So an equation with bars splits into two cases. The inside equals the right side, or the inside equals minus the right side. Why minus? Because if the inside is negative six, the bars still turn it into six.

For example, the absolute value of the whole x plus three equals eight. Case one: x plus three is eight, so x is eight minus three, which is five. Case two: x plus three is negative eight, so x is negative eight minus three, which is negative eleven. We use the same inside twice, once with eight and once with negative eight.
at: Case one: x plus three is eight
Case two: x plus three is negative eight

slides.say: Let's check both. Five plus three is eight, and its absolute value is eight. Negative eleven plus three is negative eight, and its absolute value is eight too. Both work.

There's also a picture for this. The absolute value of the whole x minus four is the distance between x and four. You'll see why in the first questions. For now, one example. The absolute value of the whole x minus four equals two means that x is two steps from four. Two steps to the right is six, and two steps to the left is two.
at: the distance between x and four
Two steps to the right is six
two steps to the left is two

slides.say: So x is six or two. Six minus four is two, and two minus four is negative two, and both have an absolute value of two.
at: So x is six or two

slides: Inequalities are a little harder. There are two situations: the bars are on the big side of the inequality, or on the small side. And with the absolute value of x, the range is always symmetric. What works on the positive side works on the negative side too.

slides.say: The absolute value of x is bigger than three. Without its sign, x must be more than three. Four and five work. Negative four and negative five work too, because the bars remove the minus. And two? Its absolute value is two, which is not bigger than three, so two doesn't work.
at: The absolute value of x is bigger than three

slides.say: On the number line, that's two rays going outward, one from three to the right, and one from negative three to the left. The circles are open, because three itself is not bigger than three. So bars on the big side give an open range: x is bigger than three, or x is smaller than negative three.
at: one from three to the right
one from negative three to the left
So bars on the big side

slides.say: Now the absolute value of x is smaller than three. Without its sign, x must be less than three. Two, one and zero work, and so do negative one and negative two. Negative five? No. The bars turn it into five, which is not smaller than three.
at: Now the absolute value of x is smaller than three

slides.say: On the number line, that's one band between negative three and three. So bars on the small side give a closed range: x is between negative three and three. It's just like the x squared inequalities you learned. On the small side the range is closed, and on the big side it's open.
at: So bars on the small side
x is between negative three and three

slides.say: With an expression inside, it's the same idea. The absolute value of the whole x minus two is smaller than five. The bars are on the small side, so the inside, x minus two, is between negative five and five. Now add two to all three parts. Negative five plus two is negative three, and five plus two is seven. So x is between negative three and seven.
at: The absolute value of the whole x minus two
So x is between negative three and seven

slides: So bars show up in expressions, in equations and in inequalities. Inside first, then the bars, and the result is never negative. Equations split into two cases, and inequalities give a closed range or an open one. And like in almost every topic, plugging in a number works here too. [pause] Okay. I'll see you in the next video.
